snacks.title: Survival Basics
snacks.canDo: Get through the first day politely before you can build long sentences.

word.nuance: 안녕하세요 is the all-purpose 존댓말 greeting for strangers, coworkers, shopkeepers, teachers — basically any adult you are not on 반말 terms with. The root 안녕(安寧) means 'peace/well-being', so the phrase literally asks 'are you at peace?', but modern Koreans hear it simply as 'hello'; it works morning, noon, and night since Korean has no separate 'good morning/afternoon/evening' equivalents. The register ladder runs: 안녕 (반말, close friends / children / clear juniors) → 안녕하세요 (standard polite) → 안녕하십니까 (격식체, formal broadcasts and service settings). A key social rule: saying 안녕 to a teacher, boss, or older stranger signals either extreme intimacy or disrespect — always default to 안녕하세요 until 반말 is mutually established. The classic English-speaker trap is splitting greetings by time of day or tacking on 어떻게 지내세요? every time — in Korean, 안녕하세요 alone is the complete, natural hello, and opening with a wellbeing question to a stranger sounds oddly probing.

감사합니다 is the default 존댓말 'thank you' safe with literally anyone — a stranger, a clerk, a teacher, your boss — and never wrong. It comes from Sino-Korean 감사(感謝), giving it a slightly formal, composed feel compared to the warmer native alternative 고맙습니다. The formality ladder runs: 고마워 (반말, friends/juniors) → 고마워요 (gentle polite) → 감사합니다 (standard polite) → 대단히 감사합니다 / 감사드립니다 (격식, speeches, written). The nearest alternative is 고맙습니다, which is pure native Korean and sounds a touch warmer and more personal; both are equally polite, and the choice is mostly about tone rather than rank. The classic English-speaker error is stacking a noun directly: you cannot say '도움 감사합니다' as if words simply pile up — to thank for an action you must attach ~아/어 주셔서 (도와주셔서 감사합니다). Another mistake is using 고마워 with strangers or anyone older, which sounds presumptuous and rude.

죄송합니다 is the higher-deference 'I'm sorry', from Sino-Korean 죄송(罪悚), literally 'I feel I have committed a fault and am fearful before you'. That deferential weight makes it the correct apology toward strangers, seniors, customers, and your boss — situations where showing you lower yourself is required. The formality ladder: 미안해 (반말, peers/friends) → 미안해요 (gentle polite) → 죄송해요 / 죄송합니다 (polite, upward-safe) → 대단히 죄송합니다 / 죄송스럽습니다 (격식, serious fault). The dividing line versus 미안하다 is deference: 죄송하다 lowers yourself and is always safe upward; 미안하다 is more horizontal and personal, and sounds too casual to a boss. Three concrete English-speaker mistakes: (1) attaching the reason wrong — use X-아/어서 죄송합니다 (늦어서 죄송합니다), not '늦은 것 죄송'; (2) using 미안해 to a boss or stranger; (3) confusing it with 실례합니다, which is 'excuse me' for a small intrusion, not an apology for fault.
네 can also mean “I hear you” or “okay” while listening, not only yes.
Use 아니요 as a polite no. 아니 is casual, and 아니요 often sounds softer when followed by a short explanation like 괜찮아요 or 몰라요.

word.en: Goodbye (said by the person who is leaving).
word.nuance: 안녕히 계세요 is the mirror image of 안녕히 가세요: you say it when YOU are the one leaving and the other person STAYS. The pivot is the verb — 계시다 is the honorific of 있다 'to be/remain (of a person)', so 계세요 wishes the one staying to 'remain in peace'. Both phrases share the same 안녕(安寧) 'peace' root; the verb alone signals direction. English speakers reliably swap the two because 'goodbye' has no who-moves information — the one-second fix is: if my feet are moving, use 계세요; if their feet are moving, use 가세요. A smooth social move before departing is to add 먼저 갈게요 or 먼저 가 볼게요 ('I'll head off first') so leaving ahead of others doesn't seem abrupt or rude. When leaving a workplace where colleagues are still working, pairing 안녕히 계세요 with 수고하세요 ('keep up the good work') is the natural and considerate exit. Formal register: 안녕히 계십시오.

snacks.canDo: Stay calm when you do not understand, need help, or need one practical sentence fast.

word.nuance: 한국어를 잘 못해요 = 한국어 (Korean language) + 를 (object marker) + 잘 (well) + 못하다 (to be unable to do well). The key interpretive point: 잘 못하다 means 'can't do it well' (ability is limited), while 안 하다 means 'I don't do it' (by choice). Using 안 하다 — 한국어를 안 해요 — implies you are refusing or unwilling, which is not what you mean. The 잘 softens the claim from 'I can't speak Korean at all' (한국어 못해요) to 'I'm not good at it', which is more accurate and humble. 한국어 is the neutral/formal word for the language, while 한국말 is more colloquial and warm; both are correct. The classic follow-up toolkit: 천천히 말씀해 주세요 ('please speak slowly'), 다시 한 번 말씀해 주시겠어요? ('could you say that again?'), and 영어 하시는 분 계세요? ('is there anyone who speaks English?'). English speakers most often get the particle wrong (한국어가 잘 못해요 — the language is the object, not the subject) or write 잘못해요 as one word, which means 'to do something wrong/make a mistake' — a completely different word.

snacks.title: Numbers Starter
snacks.canDo: Read prices, counts, simple dates, and clock-hour basics without waiting for a full number chapter.

word.nuance: 하나 is the native-Korean (고유어) word for "one," the counting system Koreans use for tangible things, people, age, and the clock hour — as opposed to its Sino-Korean twin 일, which rules dates, money, minutes, and phone numbers. The single biggest fact to internalize: when 하나 sits directly in front of a counter (개, 명, 시, 살, 마리), it loses its last syllable and becomes 한 — 한 개, 한 명, 한 시 — while the full 하나 only stands alone (as in counting "하나, 둘" or taking a particle, 하나만). English speakers reliably trip here by saying 하나 개 or, worse, importing the Sino number and saying 일 개; both sound clearly wrong to a Korean ear. There is no hanja because it is purely native, so do not look for one.

둘 is native-Korean "two," used for counting concrete things, people, and the clock hour, in contrast to Sino 이 which handles minutes, money, floors, and dates. Like 하나→한, 둘 contracts before a counter, dropping its final ㄹ to become 두: 두 개, 두 시, 두 명, 두 잔. The bare 둘 survives only when it stands alone or takes a particle — note the very common 둘 다 ('both') and 둘 중에 ('between the two'). English speakers often forget the contraction and say 둘 개, or reach for the Sino 이 (이 개), both of which sound off; they also tend to say 두 다 by mistake, but the fixed idiom is 둘 다. It is a pure native word, so it has no hanja.

sentence.en: Which of the two do you like more?

word.nuance: 셋 is native-Korean "three," the form used to count objects, people, and the clock hour, while Sino 삼 covers minutes, money, dates, and floors. Before a counter it contracts to 세 (세 개, 세 시, 세 명, 세 권), and the bare 셋 only appears standalone, with a particle, or in the social phrase 셋이서 ('as three people together'). A frequent English-speaker error is leaving it uncontracted as 셋 개 or borrowing Sino 삼 개; both are immediately wrong to natives. Another subtle pitfall: 세 (three) and 네 (four) look and sound similar, so learners mix them up — keep 세=3, 네=4 firmly apart. 셋 is purely native and has no hanja.

sentence.en: I'll count to three. One, two, three!
There are six pieces of candy.

word.nuance: 열 (熱, the hanja for 'heat') is a fever, and the must-learn collocation is 열이 나다, where 나다 literally means '(something) comes out/arises' — Korean conceives a fever as heat 'coming out' of the body, so you never say 열을 가지다 ('have/possess a fever'), a direct translation of English 'have' that sounds completely unnatural. You can also say 열이 있다 ('there is fever') as a calmer alternative. The level of a fever is described with 높다/낮다 (열이 높다 = high fever), not 크다/작다, and once treated, 열이 내리다 ('the fever comes down') is the natural way to say it subsides — paralleling how prices or temperature 내리다. To take someone's temperature is 열을 재다 (재다 = to measure), the same verb as 키를 재다 (measure height). Don't confuse this 열 with the homonym 열 meaning 'ten' (열 개 = ten items); context separates them.

sentence.en: Count to ten and open your eyes.

word.nuance: 일 is the Sino-Korean (漢字語) number "one," from the hanja 一 (a single horizontal stroke). It governs the abstract/measured world: dates, money (원), minutes, phone numbers, floors, bus and problem numbers, and any count from the hundreds up — the exact opposite of native 하나, which counts tangible things, people, and the clock hour. So one o'clock is 한 시 but one minute is 일 분; one apple is 사과 한 개 but one won is 일 원. English speakers, used to a single set of numbers, constantly blur the line — saying 일 시 for one o'clock or 하나 분 for one minute. A handy memory hook: anything that already feels like a 'code' or a 'measurement' (clock minutes, addresses, prices) is Sino 일.

이 is the Sino-Korean number "two," from the hanja 二 (two horizontal strokes). It runs dates, money, minutes, floors, math, and counts in the hundreds and up — versus native 둘/두, which counts physical things, people, and the clock hour. So two o'clock is 두 시 but two minutes is 이 분; two cups is 두 잔 but two won is 이 원. A real trap unique to 이: it is identical in sound to the demonstrative 이 ('this') and the subject/topic particle context around it, so 이 분 can mean either 'two minutes' or 'this person' (분 = honorific 'person') depending on context — listen carefully. English speakers also tend to use native 둘 for prices or floors (둘 층); those are Sino: 이 층. Treat measured, coded things as Sino 이.

삼 is the Sino-Korean number "three," from the hanja 三 (three horizontal strokes). It governs dates, money, minutes, floors, arithmetic, and larger counts — in contrast to native 셋/세, which counts tangible objects, people, and the clock hour. So three o'clock is 세 시 but three minutes is 삼 분; three notebooks is 세 권 but 30,000 won is 삼만 원. The recurring English-speaker mistake is using 삼 to tell the hour (삼 시) or reaching for native 세 in a price (세만 원). A useful anchor: cooking and timer durations in minutes are always Sino, so '3 minutes' on a ramen pack is 삼 분, never 세 분. Keep measured/coded contexts on the Sino side, 삼.

sentence.en: Lend me just a thousand won.

snacks.title: Family Words
snacks.canDo: Name close people naturally when introducing yourself or asking about someone.

word.nuance: 가족 is the Sino-Korean word 家族 ('house' 家 + 'clan/group' 族), so it names the whole family unit as a collective, never a single relative — for one member you must say 가족 한 명 or name the relationship (형, 누나). The near-synonym 식구 also means family but literally means 食口 'mouths to feed', stressing the people who live and eat under one roof, so 식구 feels warmer and more domestic ('우리 식구 다섯이에요') while 가족 is the neutral standard term that also covers relatives living apart. Register is neutral and safe in any setting. The big English-speaker trap is two-fold: 'big/small family' is 가족이 많다/적다 (many/few), never 가족이 크다 (that sounds like physically large bodies); and Koreans say 우리 가족 ('our family') where English forces 'my family', so the 우리 is idiomatic, not a mistake.

sentence.en: My dad works at a company.

word.nuance: 어머니 is the respectful, neutral word for 'mother,' used in polite speech, in writing, and when talking about your mom to others. Its near-synonym 엄마 is the affectionate home word ('mom/mommy') that people usually call her directly at home, while 어머니 carries more formality and respect — the same distance as English 'mom' vs 'mother.' The higher honorific 어머님 is for someone else's mother or your mother-in-law. As an elder, 어머니 routinely takes honorific particles and endings: 께서 for the subject, 께 for 'to,' and -(으)시- verbs (하세요, 주무세요). Watch two English-speaker traps: the copula contracts to 어머니예요 after the vowel 니 (not '어머니이에요'); and you give things to her with the honorific 어머니께 ... 드리다, not the plain 어머니한테 ... 줘요. Possession is likewise 우리 어머니, since 내 어머니 sounds unnaturally distant.

아버지 is the respectful, neutral word for 'father,' used in polite conversation, in writing, and whenever you speak about your dad to others. Its near-synonym 아빠 is the warm home word ('dad/daddy'): children and many adults call him 아빠 to his face, while 아버지 sounds more grown-up, dignified, or formal — the gap is exactly the English 'dad' vs 'father.' One step higher is 아버님, reserved for someone else's father or your father-in-law. Because a father is an elder, 아버지 naturally pulls honorific machinery: the subject marker 께서, the dative 께, and -(으)시- verb endings (읽으세요, 주무세요). Two English-speaker pitfalls: the copula is 아버지예요 (vowel-final 지 → 예요, not '아버지이에요'); and possession uses 우리 아버지 ('our father'), since 내 아버지 sounds oddly cold to Korean ears.

sentence.en: My father is an office worker.

word.nuance: 언니 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older sister, and it extends warmly to any close older woman — an older female friend, a senior at school or work — and is also the friendly way younger women address a female shopkeeper or restaurant server ('언니, 여기요!'), so it ranges from blood sister to polite stranger. Its gendered counterpart is 누나, used by a MALE for the same older-sister bond, so 언니 vs 누나 splits purely by the speaker's gender, and the word reveals that the speaker is a woman — a distinction English 'older sister' simply lacks. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 endings, and 언니 itself serves as the address (you say 언니, not her name). The chief English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나, never 언니, for an older sister; and don't be surprised to hear women call a saleswoman 언니 — it is friendly social lubricant, not a claim of kinship.

오빠 is the word a FEMALE uses for an older brother, and it is the most socially loaded kinship term in Korean: a woman also calls a close older male friend, a senior, or especially a boyfriend 오빠, so '오빠' on its own can mean 'my big brother', 'my guy friend', or 'babe' depending on context — hence 친오빠 exists to specify the actual sibling. Its gendered counterpart is 형, used by a MALE for the same older-brother relationship, so 오빠 vs 형 splits by speaker, and the word instantly reveals the speaker is a woman. Register is casual and affectionate, used with -요 forms, and 오빠 is itself the address term (never his bare name). The major English-speaker pitfall is gender — a man must say 형, never 오빠 — and the cultural trap: because 오빠 also means 'boyfriend' in romantic use, calling a male friend 오빠 can imply flirtation, so learners should know the connotation before using it freely.

누나 is the word a MALE uses for an older sister, and like 형 it doubles as a warm address title a younger man uses for any older woman he is close to — an older female friend, senior student, or, famously, a beloved older woman ('누나' in K-pop). Its gendered partner is 언니, which a FEMALE uses for the very same older-sister relationship, so 누나 vs 언니 is split purely by who is speaking, and the word betrays the speaker's gender in a way English 'older sister' cannot. Register is casual but deferential: 누나 is itself a respectful address (you call her 누나, not her name) and you speak up to her with -요 forms. A very natural collocation is 도와주다 'help (as a favor)'. The headline English-speaker pitfall is gender: a man must say 누나 and a woman 언니 for an older sister — swapping them is an immediate giveaway — and remember 누나 is also how a younger man fondly addresses an older woman, not only a sibling.

형 (Sino-Korean 兄 'elder brother') is the word a MALE uses for an older brother, and crucially it is also a warm address term a younger man uses for any slightly-older male he is close to — an older friend, schoolmate, or colleague — so '민수 형' can mean 'Minsu, my big-brother-figure', not a blood relative. The matched set is gendered by speaker: a female says 오빠 for the same older-brother relationship, while 누나/언니 cover older sisters — so the single word leaks the speaker's gender, something English's flat 'older brother' never does. Register is casual-but-respectful: 형 is itself an honorific address (you call him 형, never his bare name), and you speak up to him. The dominant English-speaker pitfall is gender: a woman must never call her older brother 형 — that is 오빠 — and second, don't assume 형 always means kin; in daily life it is most often the affectionate title for an older male friend.

동생 (Sino-Korean 同生 'born of the same' parents) means a younger sibling and, unlike the older-sibling words, is NOT split by speaker gender and does NOT itself reveal whether the sibling is male or female — to specify you prepend 남 (男) for 남동생 'younger brother' or 여 (女) for 여동생 'younger sister'. It also extends to any younger person you are close to (a junior at work or school), mirroring how 형/오빠/누나/언니 work upward; the system is asymmetric — elders get gendered, speaker-dependent titles, while juniors share the one neutral 동생. Register: unlike the older-sibling titles, 동생 is NOT used as a direct address — you call a younger sibling by name, and 동생 is only how you refer to them. The key English-speaker pitfall is assuming 동생 means 'younger brother'; it is sex-neutral, so without 남/여 it could be either, and you should never address someone as '동생' the way you'd say '형' — call them by name instead.

할머니 is your grandmother on either side, and in plain conversation Koreans use it for both the father's and the mother's mother; add 외- (외할머니) or 친- (친할머니) only when you must mark the side. It is built from 할- (an old prefix meaning a generation above) + 어머니 'mother', and it doubles as a warm, respectful way to address ANY elderly woman you feel close to, much like English 'grandma' for a kindly neighbor. The big trap for English speakers is grammar of respect, not vocabulary: a grandmother is a high-status elder, so the verb itself must be honorific — say 할머니는 사세요 / 주무세요 / 드세요, never the flat 살아요 / 자요 / 먹어요. Pair it with 우리 할머니 ('our grandmother'), not 제 할머니, because Korean treats family as shared. Compared with the polite stranger-address 아주머니/아주머님 (a middle-aged woman), 할머니 implies real old age, so misjudging the age can sting.

할아버지 is your grandfather on either side, and casual speech uses it for both the father's and the mother's father; 외할아버지 (maternal) or 친할아버지 (paternal) pin down the side when it matters. It is 할- (a prefix for the generation above) + 아버지 'father', and like 할머니 it can respectfully address any elderly man you know. The spelling trips beginners because of the liaison: it is one solid word, 할아버지, written together — never 할 아버지 — and the ㄹ slides onto the next syllable so it sounds like 하라버지. The deeper pitfall for English speakers is honorifics: a grandfather outranks you, so the verb climbs to the honorific level (읽으세요, 주무세요, 진지 드세요), and 밥 politely becomes 진지. Say 우리 할아버지, mirroring 우리 할머니, rather than the textbook-literal 제 할아버지.

snacks.title: Body Basics
snacks.canDo: Say what hurts, describe people, and understand basic health phrases.

word.nuance: 몸 is the physical body taken as a whole, and crucially it's also the word Koreans reach for to describe how they FEEL: 몸이 아파요 (sick) and 몸이 안 좋아요 (off/unwell) are the everyday health phrases. The near-synonym is the Sino-Korean 신체(身體, 'body-substance'), but 신체 is clinical/official — 신체검사 (physical exam), 신체 활동 (physical activity) — and sounds stiff if you use it about yourself, so say 몸. Habitual collocations: 몸이 아프다, 몸이 안 좋다, 몸이 피곤하다, 몸이 무겁다, 몸조심하다, 몸이 약하다 (to have a weak constitution). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle and the verb: you say 몸이 아프다 ('the body is sick'), so the body is the SUBJECT (이/가) — never 몸을 아파요. Also don't directly translate 'my body is heavy' as a weight statement; 몸이 무겁다 means you feel sluggish/lethargic, not that you weigh a lot.

머리 covers both the head and the hair on it, and only context (the verb or adjective) tells them apart: 머리가 아프다 = head hurts, but 머리가 길다 / 머리를 감다 = hair. The strict word for a single strand is 머리카락, yet in speech Koreans almost always shorten it to 머리, so 'cut my hair' is 머리를 자르다, not 머리카락을 자르다. The pitfall for English speakers is the washing verb: hair takes 감다 (머리를 감다), never the 씻다 you use for hands or face, so 머리를 씻다 sounds childish or wrong. Also note 머리가 좋다/나쁘다 is a fixed idiom for being smart/dim, not a comment on hair quality, and the body part is always marked with 가 (머리가 아파요), not 을.

얼굴 is the whole human face — both its looks and its surface you wash — and is the everyday word with no formality issue; you use it equally with friends and elders. Its near-synonym 낯 (as in 낯이 익다 'the face looks familiar', 낯설다 'unfamiliar') is old-fashioned and survives mostly in set idioms, so for plain 'face' always reach for 얼굴. Two pitfalls trip up English speakers. First, hair on the head is 감다 (감다 = wash hair) but the FACE is 씻다, the same verb as for hands and dishes — never say 얼굴을 감다. Second, English 'big face' does not transfer: a flattering 'small face' is 얼굴이 작다 (a real Korean compliment about proportion), and you do not say 얼굴이 커요 to mean handsome. Color uses 빨갛다 (얼굴이 빨개요), and to feel for fever Koreans touch the 이마, not the whole 얼굴.

sentence.en: My older sister's face is really pretty.

word.nuance: 눈 is the eye, but the identical spelling also means 'snow'; the two are split by pitch (eye = short/low, snow = long/high) and above all by context, so listeners rarely confuse them. Korean treats the pair of eyes as one uncountable 눈, so you never pluralize it. The big English-speaker trap is eyesight: vision is rated with 좋다 (good) and 나쁘다 (bad) — 눈이 좋아요 / 눈이 나빠요 — never with 'strong/weak' (강하다/약하다), which would sound bizarre. Note that 눈을 감다 uses the same 감다 as washing hair but means 'close', and the related verb 보다 ('see/look') is what the eye does, while 만나다 ('meet') is for people, so don't blend them.

코 is the nose, but cold symptoms split into precise collocations English speakers must memorize: a blocked nose is 코가 막히다 (막히다 = be blocked) and a runny nose is 콧물이 나다, where 콧물 literally stitches 코(nose)+물(water) into 'nose-water' = snot. Saying 코가 아프다 actually means the nose physically hurts (an injury), so it does NOT convey a cold — that is the classic 직역 trap. To blow your nose is 코를 풀다 (풀다 'to release/undo'); beware 코를 불다, which means to blow air out like a whistle and sounds absurd here. For looks, a tall nose bridge (admired in Korea) is 코가 높다, with 코가 낮다 as the flat-bridge opposite, paralleling how 키가 크다 works for height.

입 is the mouth, but its most useful expressions are idioms that won't survive word-for-word translation. 입에 맞다 means food 'suits your taste' (lit. 'fits the mouth') — it judges flavor, so 'this fits in my mouth' is a beginner mistranslation. 입이 짧다 ('short mouth') describes a picky or light eater, while 입이 무겁다 ('heavy mouth') means tight-lipped/discreet and 입이 가볍다 ('light mouth') means a blabbermouth — none are about physical size. To physically open the mouth is 입을 벌리다 (벌리다 = spread apart), as a dentist commands; do not use 열다 ('open' a door/box) for the mouth. Note also that 입 (mouth, the organ) is different from 말 (speech/words), so 'watch your mouth' as in language is 말조심하다, not anything with 입.

귀 is the ear, and the key English-speaker pitfall is the verb of hearing. Korean splits 듣다 (to listen actively, by choice) from 들리다 (to be heard / reach the ear, passively, beyond control). So 'I can't hear' is 귀가 안 들려요 with the passive 들리다 — using 못 듣다 implies you deliberately didn't listen, which is rude when talking about someone's deafness. There are two natural ways to describe hard-of-hearing: the plain 귀가 안 들리다 and the gentler idiom 귀가 어둡다 ('the ear is dark'), whose opposite 귀가 밝다 ('bright ear') means keen hearing. To plug your ears against noise is 귀를 막다 (막다 = block), the same 막다 as a blocked nose (코가 막히다). When speaking about elders, pair this with honorifics, e.g. 귀가 어두우세요.

목 covers both the neck and the throat, so 목이 아프다 most often means a sore throat from a cold, NOT neck pain — assuming it only means 'neck' is the main English-speaker pitfall (for true neck/shoulder stiffness Koreans more often say 목이 뻐근하다 or specify 목덜미). Thirst is the fixed phrase 목이 마르다 ('the throat dries'), where 마르다 is 르-irregular → 말라요, 말랐어요; do not invent 목이 건조하다. A swollen throat is 목이 붓다 (ㅅ-irregular → 부어요), the same swelling verb as 발이 붓다, and going hoarse is 목이 쉬다 (lit. 'the throat rests'). Idiomatically 목이 빠지게 기다리다 means to wait so eagerly your neck stretches out ('wait with bated breath'). A throat/neck symptom marks the part with 가 (목이 아파요).

sentence.en: I sat for a long time so my shoulder hurts.
I carried a heavy bag so my arm hurts.

word.nuance: 손 is the hand, and the first thing to fix is the washing verb: hands take 씻다 (손을 씻다), in deliberate contrast to hair, which uses 감다 — mixing them (손을 감다) is a classic beginner slip. Beyond the literal organ, 손 powers vivid idioms that aren't about anatomy: 손이 크다 ('big hand') means generous, especially someone who cooks or gives a lot, not someone with large hands; 손이 가다 ('the hand goes') means a task or person takes a lot of effort/attention; and 손이 모자라다 ('hands are short') means short-staffed. To hold someone's hand is 손을 잡다 (잡다 = grasp), used both romantically and to guide a child across the road. Note the hand is usually the object of an action, so it pairs with 을/를 (손을 씻다, 손을 잡다) rather than 가.

sentence.en: My finger got caught in the door so it hurts.

word.nuance: 배 means the belly/stomach (the body region), and the same syllable also means 'pear' and 'boat/ship' — three homonyms split only by context. Hunger and fullness are locked set phrases that ALWAYS keep 배: 배가 고프다 (hungry) and 배가 부르다 (full); you cannot say 나는 고파요 alone, which is the top beginner error. Both adjectives are irregular: 고프다 is ㅡ-irregular (고파요, 고팠어요) and 부르다 is 르-irregular (불러요, 불렀어요). Note 배 here is the colloquial stomach for aches and hunger, distinct from the Sino-Korean 위 (胃, the actual stomach organ) used in medical contexts like 위염 (gastritis). A culturally important idiom: 배가 아프다 also figuratively means to be jealous of someone's good fortune ('my stomach hurts' = green with envy), so context decides literal pain vs. envy.

sentence.en: I climbed a lot of stairs so my knee hurts.

word.nuance: 발 is specifically the foot — the part below the ankle — and Korean keeps it strictly separate from 다리 (the leg, the whole limb above), so pointing at your ankle and saying 다리 is wrong; that is the core mix-up for English speakers who blur 'leg/foot'. Useful collocations: 발을 다치다 (injure the foot, with 다치다 taking 을/를) and 발이 붓다 (the foot swells), where 붓다 is a ㅅ-irregular verb that drops ㅅ before a vowel → 부어요, 부었어요, not 붓어요. Idiomatically 발이 넓다 ('wide foot') means well-connected with a broad social network, never literally big feet (for that you'd say 발이 크다). When you cause an injury yourself, prefer the active 다치다 (발을 다쳤어요) over a passive construction.

snacks.title: Time And Days
snacks.canDo: Understand today, tomorrow, weekdays, and simple appointment timing.

word.nuance: 오늘 usually does not need 에. 오늘에 sounds unnatural for ordinary “today.”

어제 is a native deictic time word meaning 'yesterday', sitting in the set 그저께(엊그제) 'day before yesterday' – 어제 – 오늘 'today' – 내일 'tomorrow' – 모레 'day after tomorrow'. Its defining grammar quirk is that, like 오늘 and 내일, it normally takes NO 에: you say 어제 만났어요, never 어제에. (The particle reappears only when 어제 combines with a sub-period, e.g. 어제 아침에, where 에 attaches to 아침.) 어제 naturally pairs with past tense — 았어요/었어요 — so it's a reliable signal that the verb should be past. Habitual partners: 어제 아침/저녁, 어제부터, 어제 일 'yesterday's matter', 어제 본/한/간 + noun. The big English-speaker pitfall is over-marking with 에 by analogy to 'on' or to other time nouns like 주말에; bare 어제 is correct. A second trap is pairing 어제 with present or future tense; because it's firmly past, 어제 가요 is wrong — it must be 어제 갔어요.
내일 is a time word, so it can appear naturally without 에.
지금 usually comes near the beginning of the sentence or before the verb phrase.

아침 is a native Korean word that does double duty: the early part of the day (roughly sunrise to mid-morning) and the breakfast meal — the same way English 'morning' differs from the meal but Korean merges the breakfast sense into the time word. The grammar disambiguates: with 에 (아침에) it's the time, with 을 (아침을 먹다) it's the food. Contrast 아침 vs 오전: 아침 is the felt, lived early morning, while 오전 午前 is the neutral clock-AM you put on timetables — so 아침에 일어나요 (waking life) but 오전 9시 회의 (a scheduled item). Habitual partners: 아침에 일어나다/운동하다, 아침을 먹다/거르다 ('skip breakfast'), 아침 일찍, 매일 아침. The big English-speaker pitfall is using 오전 for the breakfast meal — 오전 is only the clock period and can never name food, so 'eat breakfast' must be 아침을 먹다, never 오전을 먹다. Also don't force 에 onto the meal sense: you eat 아침을, you don't 'eat at morning'.

sentence.en: I drink coffee in the morning.

word.nuance: 저녁 is a native Korean word covering the early-night period AND the dinner meal, mirroring 아침/점심: 저녁을 먹다 is the food, 저녁에 is the time. The fine line is 저녁 vs 밤: 저녁 is the social early evening — dusk through dinner, when people are still out — whereas 밤 is true late night when it's dark and quiet; so a 7 p.m. dinner is 저녁, but 11 p.m. is 밤. 저녁 also contrasts with the clock label 오후, which ends as 저녁 begins. Habitual partners: 저녁을 먹다, 저녁 식사, 저녁 약속, 저녁 메뉴, 저녁에 만나다. The main English-speaker pitfall is using 밤 for the dinner meal because 'night' feels close — but 'eat dinner' is 저녁을 먹다, never 밤을 먹다 (밤 can't name a meal, and 밤 also happens to mean 'chestnut'). A second trap: don't mark the dinner-meal with 에; you eat 저녁을, while 저녁에 means 'in the evening (do something)'.

sentence.en: I watch a movie in the evening.

word.nuance: 주말 is Sino-Korean, 週末 — 週 'week' + 末 'end', literally 'week-end', and its opposites are 평일 平日 'weekday' and 주중 週中 'midweek'. It refers to Saturday and Sunday as a block. The contrast worth noting is 주말 vs 휴일: 주말 is specifically the weekend, while 휴일 休日 is any day off including public holidays — so a Wednesday holiday is a 휴일 but not a 주말. Habitual partners: 주말에 쉬다/놀다, 이번/지난/다음 주말, 주말마다, 즐거운 주말, and the farewell 주말 잘 보내세요. The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: learners borrow 'at/on' loosely and write 주말에서, but 에서 marks a LOCATION or a source ('from'); the time-when always takes 에 → 주말에. A second subtlety: for 'this weekend' use 이번 주말 (이번 = the current instance), not 오늘 주말; and 다음 주말 'next weekend' vs 다음 주 주말 can differ, so keep 다음 주말 for the upcoming Sat–Sun.

sentence.en: I usually rest on the weekend.
The day after tomorrow is Thursday.

word.nuance: 시간 works with 있어요/없어요 and is essential for scheduling.

분 is the time unit 'minute', written with the hanja 分 (to divide/a part) — a minute being a division of the hour. The crucial rule: 분 ALWAYS takes Sino-Korean numbers (일·이·삼·사·오·...), so it's 오 분, 삼십 분, never the native 하나·둘·셋. This creates Korea's famous mixed clock, where the HOUR uses native numbers + 시 (한 시, 두 시) but the MINUTE uses Sino numbers + 분 (십 분, 삼십 분): 한 시 십 분 = 1:10. Note 분 also means 'a respected person' (한 분 = one person, honorific) and is the honorific counter for people — same syllable, totally different word, disambiguated by context. The English-speaker pitfall: applying the native numbers used for 시 to 분 as well (✗한 분 for one minute — that actually means 'one person, honorific'); the correct 'one minute' is 일 분. Collocates with 후/전 (after/before), 동안 (for), 정도 (about), 만 (only), and 걸리다 (to take).

snacks.title: People And Places
snacks.canDo: Recognize the people and places that appear in first conversations and errands.

word.nuance: 사람 can mean one person or people in general. It is useful for describing crowds, identity, and who someone is.
친구 can mean friend or same-age peer depending on context.
학생 is a common identity word. Use 이에요 after 학생 because it ends in a consonant.
님 makes the word respectful. 선생님 is also used as a polite title.

의사 is Sino-Korean 醫師 ('medicine' 醫 + 'master/teacher' 師), so the word literally frames a doctor as a master of medicine — which is why Koreans almost reflexively append 선생님 (의사 선생님) when addressing or referring to one, the way English keeps 'Doctor' as a title. Saying bare 의사 to or about a specific physician can sound flat or even slightly disrespectful, like calling them 'the doc'. Distinguish 의사 (the licensed physician) from 의자 'chair', which differs by a single vowel and trips up beginners constantly, and from 환자 'patient' and 간호사 'nurse', the other people in the room. The natural verb is 환자를 보다 ('see patients') or 진료를 보다/받다, never the English-style '의사를 하다'; a doctor 의사가 되다 ('becomes' a doctor), with the goal marked by 가, not 을.

회사원 is 會社員 ('company-member'), literally a member of a company, and it is the neutral catch-all a salaried employee of a private firm gives when asked 무슨 일 하세요? Contrast it with 직장인, which means 'a working person' in general (anyone with a paid job, including teachers or nurses): every 회사원 is a 직장인, but not every 직장인 is a 회사원. Also separate it from 사업가, the owner who runs the business — a 회사원 is employed by someone else. The pitfall for English speakers is twofold: 회사원 ends in a consonant so the copula is 회사원이에요, never 'office worker'-style 회사원예요; and don't translate 'I work at a company' as a job title — to name the job you simply say 회사원이에요 rather than literally rendering the English sentence.
학교 is one of the clearest words for practicing 에 vs 에서.
회사 often means workplace in daily conversation, not only the company as an organization.
병원 can mean hospital or clinic in everyday Korean.

sentence.en: I am sick, so I go to the hospital.

word.nuance: 식당 is 食堂 — 食 'eat' + 堂 'hall' — an 'eating hall', i.e. an ordinary, everyday place to have a meal: a neighborhood eatery, a noodle shop, or a 구내식당(cafeteria). The register contrast is 레스토랑, the loanword reserved for fancier, often Western, sit-down dining; you'd call a humble 백반집 a 식당, never a 레스토랑, and a candlelit Italian place a 레스토랑, not a plain 식당. The crucial grammar point is particle choice: use 에서 for an action done there (식당에서 먹어요 'eat AT the restaurant') but 에 for it as a destination (식당에 가요 'go TO the restaurant'). The English-speaker pitfall is exactly this 에/에서 split, since English 'at/to' don't map one-to-one; another is reaching for 레스토랑 as the default word for any restaurant when 식당 is the everyday term.

sentence.en: Let's eat lunch at this restaurant.

word.nuance: 카페 is a loanword (from French/English 'café') meaning a coffee shop — but in Korea it is as much a social and study space as a place to drink coffee; people sit for hours to chat, work on laptops, or go on a 카페 투어 of photogenic spots. The key contrast learners blur is 카페 vs 커피: 카페 is the *place*, 커피 is the *drink*, so '커피 마시러 카페에 가요' (go to the cafe to drink coffee). It overlaps with 커피숍 and the older 다방 (a dated tea-room), but 카페 is the modern default. Being borrowed, it has no hanja. The English-speaker pitfall is exactly that 카페/커피 mix-up, plus the particles — 카페에 가요 for going there but 카페에서 공부해요 for doing something there — and remember the purpose marker for 'to go drink coffee' is the verb stem + ~(으)러: 커피 마시러 카페에 가요.
화장실 is the normal public word for bathroom/restroom.

snacks.title: Home And Things
snacks.canDo: Talk about your room, belongings, and everyday objects around you.

word.nuance: 집 can mean home or house. 집에 often means “home” in movement/location sentences.

방 is the Sino-Korean character 房 ('room, chamber') and is the all-purpose word for any enclosed room, and it builds dozens of everyday compounds: 안방 (master/main room), 공부방 (study room), 노래방 (singing room/karaoke), 찜질방 (Korean sauna room), and PC방 (internet cafe). The key contrast to fix in your head is 방 vs 집: 집 is the whole house/home, but 방 is just one room inside it, so 'I'm going home' must be 집에 가요, never 방에 가요. The grammar trap is the 에 vs 에서 split: merely being located in the room uses 에 (방에 있어요 = it's in the room), but any action carried out inside the room uses 에서 (방에서 공부해요 = I study in my room) — English 'in the room' blurs both, and overusing 에 for actions is the #1 beginner error. Collocations: 방을 치우다/정리하다 (tidy the room), 방이 좁다 (the room is cramped). Register is fully neutral, used by everyone.

sentence.en: There's a laptop on the desk.

word.nuance: 의자 is Sino-Korean 椅子 ('chair') and covers any seat with legs — dining chairs, office chairs (사무용 의자 or 사무 의자), folding chairs (접이식 의자). The single most common English-speaker error is the particle with 앉다: sitting DOWN is reaching a resting position, so it must be 의자에 앉아요 (에 = destination), not 의자에서 앉아요 — even though English 'sit ON the chair' tempts you toward a location particle. Compare with standing up, which is motion away and DOES take 에서: 의자에서 일어나요. Distinguish 의자 (chair, you sit on it) from 소파 (sofa/couch, plush multi-seat) and 책상 (desk) — beginners sometimes pair them loosely. The set phrase for offering someone a seat is 의자를 빼 드리다 (pull the chair out for them). Register is neutral.

sentence.en: Please have a seat on this chair.

sentence.ko: 저는 침대에서 안 자고 바닥에서 자요.
sentence.en: I don't sleep in a bed, I sleep on the floor.

word.nuance: 옷 is a pure native Korean word (no hanja) meaning clothes/clothing for the body, and the verb you MUST pair it with is 입다 (to wear on the torso/body) — never 신다, which is reserved for footwear on the feet (신발을 신다), nor 쓰다 (hats/glasses) nor 끼다 (gloves/rings). English 'wear/put on' covers every garment with one verb, so this split is the central pitfall: 옷을 신어요 is a classic beginner error. To take clothes off is 벗다, to change them 갈아입다. For 'these clothes look good on you,' Korean says 옷이 잘 어울려요 (the clothes suit you), not a direct translation of 'you look good.' Note 옷 is treated as singular/uncountable grammatically (no plural needed): one outfit or a wardrobe full is still just 옷. The dressier counterpart 의상 (costume/attire, 衣裳) is for performances or formal contexts. Register is neutral and everyday.

sentence.en: Please take your shoes off when you come in.
I put the book into the bag.

word.nuance: 책 is useful with 읽다, 사다, 있다, and 없다. It also helps beginners practice object marker 을 because 책 ends in a consonant.

sentence.en: I write my name with a pen.
One moment, let me turn on the computer.

word.nuance: 우산 is Sino-Korean 雨傘, literally 雨 'rain' + 傘 'umbrella/parasol' — so the word transparently means 'rain-umbrella', which is your built-in reminder it's for rain. The verb is the deceptively busy 쓰다: to put up/use an umbrella is 우산을 쓰다, the same 쓰다 that covers wearing a hat (모자를 쓰다) and glasses (안경을 쓰다) — Korean groups 'things over your head/face' under 쓰다, distinct from 입다 (clothes on the torso/legs) and 신다 (footwear). The contrast to file away is 우산 vs 양산: both are 傘, but 우산 (雨傘) is the rain umbrella while 양산 (陽傘, 'sun-shade') is a parasol against sunlight — different words for different weather. Useful collocations: 우산을 쓰다/접다/펴다 (put up / fold / open an umbrella), 우산을 챙기다 (remember to grab an umbrella), 우산을 깜빡하다 (forget the umbrella). A folding umbrella is 접는 우산 or 3단 우산, a long one 장우산. Pitfall: English 'wear/carry an umbrella' must become 쓰다 (use over the head), never 입다, and don't reuse 우산 for a sun parasol — that's 양산.

sentence.en: It's raining. Do you have an umbrella?

word.nuance: 돈 is money. In stores, 카드 and 현금 are often more specific and useful.

snacks.title: Food Basics
snacks.canDo: Read menus and say simple food preferences or restrictions.

word.nuance: 밥 literally is the bowl of cooked white rice, but by extension it is the default word for 'a meal' — which is why 밥 먹었어요? functions as a real greeting like 'how are you?', not a literal question about rice. Contrast it with 식사(食事), the polite Sino-Korean word for 'a meal': you offer an elder 식사하셨어요?, never the blunt 밥 먹었어요?. The verb is 먹다(eat), and to cook rice you say 밥을 하다 or 밥을 짓다, not 밥을 만들다. The big English-speaker pitfall is hearing 밥 only as 'rice' and missing that 밥 먹자 means 'let's grab a bite', and that to a boss you must upgrade to 식사 to stay polite.

sentence.en: I eat rice in the morning.

word.nuance: 물 is essential in restaurants. 물 주세요 is more useful than just knowing “water.”

In everyday speech 고기 by default means red land meat — usually 돼지고기(pork) or 소고기(beef) — so 고기 먹으러 가자 implies a BBQ, not seafood. To be specific you compound the animal onto 고기: 닭고기(chicken), 소고기(beef), 돼지고기(pork). The words to contrast are 생선(fish as food) and 해산물(seafood), which Koreans do NOT file under 고기; chicken sits on the edge, so people usually say 닭고기 rather than bare 고기 for it. The set cooking verb is 굽다, a ㅂ-irregular that becomes 구워요/구웠어요 (not 'gubeoyo'). The English-speaker pitfall is the English umbrella sense of 'meat' that includes fish and poultry — in Korean, unmarked 고기 leans strongly toward pork/beef, and you should name the animal when you mean otherwise.

sentence.en: I want to eat meat tonight.
I eat a lot of vegetables.
I eat bread in the morning.
How much is a tray of eggs?

word.nuance: In speech, 커피 마셔요 without 를 is also natural, but learn the full frame first.

차 (茶) is the Sino-Korean word for 'tea,' the brewed leaf or herbal drink, and because it is a beverage it must pair with 마시다 (to drink), never 먹다 (to eat) — though casual speakers do say 차를 먹다 colloquially, learners should default to 마시다. The same syllable 차 (車) also means 'car/vehicle,' so only context separates 차를 마시다 (drink tea) from 차를 타다 (ride a car); they are written identically. Unlike English 'tea,' Korean 차 covers herbal and grain infusions too, so 보리차 (barley tea) and 옥수수차 (corn tea) are 차 even with no tea leaves. A common English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 먹다 by analogy with 'have some tea,' but in standard Korean a polite host says 차 드세요 (드시다 being the honorific of 마시다/먹다). Natural collocations include 차를 우리다 (steep tea) and 차 한 잔 하다 (literally 'do one cup of tea,' meaning to chat over tea).

sentence.en: I drink tea in the morning.
How about a glass of beer?

word.nuance: 음식 is the general word for food or cuisine. It combines naturally with Korean, spicy, delicious, and eat.

sentence.en: I want to eat Korean food.
What would you like to drink? Shall I get you a drink?

snacks.title: Color Words

word.nuance: 색깔 is the everyday, standalone word for 'color,' built on the Sino-Korean root 색 (色 'color') plus a native suffix that makes it feel fuller and more conversational. Its near-synonym is just 색: the dividing line is grammatical, not meaning — 색깔 stands on its own (색깔이 예뻐요, 무슨 색깔?), while 색 is the building block that fuses to a specific shade name (파란색 blue, 빨간색 red, 노란색 yellow). A more formal, technical synonym is 색상, common in design and shopping ('color option'). The main English-speaker pitfall is over-using 색깔 by sticking it onto shade names — '파란색깔' is wrong; the named colors take 색, giving 파란색. Also, to ask 'what color,' the natural question word is 무슨 색깔, not 어떤 색깔 (which leans toward 'what kind/sort of color').

word.en: Whoa / OMG / no way — a gut reaction of shock, disbelief, or mild dismay.
word.nuance: 헐 is a pure interjection of shock — the involuntary sound that comes out when something startling, dismaying, or unbelievable hits you. It's hugely common in texting and casual conversation among friends and younger people. Because it's a raw exclamation there is no polite form: there is no 헐요 or 헐이에요; it lives entirely in banmal territory. The dividing line against 대박 is emotional direction: 헐 carries surprise often tinged with 'oh no' or dismay, while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — that's why 헐 어떡해 (shock + worry) is a natural pair but 대박 어떡해 is odd. Also don't confuse 헐 with 헉: 헐 is drawn-out disbelief ('whoa, no way'), while 헉 is a sharp one-syllable gasp of fright or physical surprise. The English-speaker pitfall is using 헐 in a professional or respectful setting — to an elder or boss it sounds childish and rude; in those moments use 어머 for neutral surprise or a full 정말요? 그런 일이. A second pitfall is trying to write 헐요 to be polite — simply switch words.

word.en: Awesome! / wow / no way — a big reaction to something amazing, shocking, or extreme.
word.nuance: 대박 literally means 'a big hit / jackpot' (대 大 'big' + 박 = jackpot), and as a reaction it explodes out for anything extreme — amazingly good, but also shocking or unbelievably bad. It is youth slang and firmly casual: 대박 alone is banmal among friends; for even a little politeness say 대박이에요, though that still reads as informal in flavor. The variant ladder is 대박 → 대박이다 → 대박이에요 → 완전 대박 (intensified). The dividing line against 헐 is emotional direction: 헐 leans toward shock/dismay ('oh no, whoa'), while 대박 leans toward 'wow, that's enormous' — though both can appear together as 헐 대박. Because it's casual slang, the English-speaker pitfall is using it in formal or hierarchical settings — to a boss or elder, 대박 sounds flippant and disrespectful; use 대단하네요 or 굉장하네요 instead. A second pitfall is assuming it's always positive: Koreans say 대박 at a car crash too, meaning 'unbelievable/shocking.'

word.en: May I ask you for directions?
word.nuance: 직역하면 '길을 좀 여쭤볼게요' is 'I will ask you for the road a bit' — but the real function is a courteous opener before asking directions of a stranger. 여쭤보다 is the humble form of 물어보다: it lowers the speaker and elevates the listener, which is exactly right when you're asking a favor of someone you don't know. Speech level matters: with a friend or someone younger drop to the plain 물어볼게 (반말), and in a very formal setting with an elder say 말씀 좀 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식). The nearest alternative expression is 저기요, 말씀 좀 묻겠습니다, but 묻다 is neutral while 여쭤보다 actively honors the person — that humility is the real dividing line. Variant scale: 여쭤볼게요 (standard polite) → 여쭤봐도 될까요? (extra courteous, seeking permission) → 여쭤보겠습니다 (격식). The classic English-speaker mistake is launching straight into 'Where is...?' with no opener, which feels abrupt or rude; Koreans almost always cushion the question with an opener first.

sentence.ko: 저기요, 길 좀 여쭤볼게요. 서울역이 어느 쪽이에요?
sentence.en: Excuse me, may I ask for directions? Which way is Seoul Station?

word.nuance: 직역하면 'Here — how do (I/you) go?' — the real function is asking the route to a destination you're pointing at on your phone map or a written address. The key insight: 여기 ('here') works because you're showing the destination visually — it refers to the spot on your screen, not where you're physically standing, so the target becomes 'here' for both speakers. Politeness lives entirely in the ending: 가요? is the everyday polite for strangers, 가? is 반말 for friends. The closest alternative expression is 여기 어떻게 찾아가요? ('how do I find my way there'), which carries the nuance of tracking down a hard-to-find spot; plain 어떻게 가요? just asks the route. Variant scale: 가요? (polite) → 가? (반말) → 가야 돼요? (polite + worried) → 가려면 어떻게 해요? (purpose-first, at info desks). The big English-speaker mistake is translating 'How can I go?' as 어떻게 갈 수 있어요?, which asks whether it is POSSIBLE or PERMITTED — for directions, use 어떻게 가요? (how, by what route).

options: Which exit number do I go out?

word.nuance: 직역하면 'From here, is it far?' — said to a stranger or staff right after they tell you where something is, so you can decide whether to walk or take transit. 여기서 is the contracted 여기에서 marking the starting point ('from here') — the 에서 is non-negotiable because distance is measured FROM a point, not AT it. Speech level is the ending only: 멀어요? (존댓말, stranger), 멀어? (반말, friend). The near alternative expression is 여기서 가까워요?, but it is not just a synonym — 가까워요? carries a hopeful tone ('please tell me it's nearby'), while 멀어요? braces for inconvenience; that emotional lean is the true dividing line. Variant scale: 멀어요? (neutral polite) → 많이 멀어요? (worried emphasis) → 걸어서 멀어요? (mode-specific). The English-speaker error is adding an explicit subject like 그것은 멀어요? or 그 장소는 멀어요? — Korean drops the subject entirely; the bare 여기서 멀어요? is complete and natural.

word.en: Can I get there on foot?
word.nuance: 직역하면 'By walking, is it possible to go?' — said to a passerby or staff when deciding whether to walk instead of taking transit. 걸어서 is formed from 걷다 (walk) + 어서, the manner connector meaning 'by means of', so the phrase asks 'is going by walking possible?' Speech level is the ending: 갈 수 있어요? (존댓말), 갈 수 있어? (반말). The three close variants have different focuses: 갈 수 있어요? (can I / is it possible), 걸어가도 돼요? (is it okay, advisable), 갈 만해요? (is it worth the walk, a quality judgment) — 걸어가도 돼요? is the nearest alternative expression and is very commonly heard. Variant scale: 걸어서 갈 수 있어요? → 걸어가도 돼요? → 걸어서 갈 만해요? The English-speaker trap is saying 걸을 수 있어요?, which asks whether your legs work or whether you are physically capable of walking — you need the directional compound 걸어서 가다 ('walk THERE') to ask about the route. A second mistake: 걸어서 갈게요 is a statement of intent ('I'll walk'), not a question.

word.nuance: 직역하면 'How much does it take?' — the verb 걸리다 has three unrelated senses (hang, catch a disease, take time), but in a transport conversation the time sense is automatic. Speech level is the ending alone: 걸려요? (존댓말), 걸려? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 시간이 얼마나 들어요?, which uses 들다 ('go into', 'cost') and leans toward effort or resources; 걸리다 is the default for clock duration. To remove any ambiguity, add 시간이 at the front: 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? Variant scale: 걸려요? (standard polite) → 얼마나 오래 걸려요? (emphasizing expected length) → 시간이 얼마나 걸려요? (explicit, formal). Combine with a mode — 지하철로, 걸어서, 버스로 — to specify exactly what kind of time you're asking about. The frequent English-speaker error is asking 얼마예요? — that means 'how much does it cost', not 'how long'; for duration the question must be 얼마나 걸려요?. Also critical: bare 얼마 걸려요? (dropping 나) sounds truncated and unnatural.

word.en: Which exit number do I go out?
word.nuance: 직역하면 'By what number exit do I go out?' — used at subway or train stations where each exit is labelled with a number. Speech level is the ending: 나가요? (존댓말), 나가? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 몇 번 출구로 나오면 돼요? ('which exit do I come out of?'), heard constantly from local Seoulites; the dividing line between it and 나가요? is subtle — 나가다 focuses on the act of going out, while 나오다 focuses on arriving at the street-level result. Variant scale: 몇 번 출구로 나가요? → 몇 번 출구로 나가야 돼요? (urgent) → 몇 번 출구예요? (quickest, just the number). Combine with a destination: [장소] 가려면 몇 번 출구로 나가요? The English-speaker mistake is asking 어느 출구로 나가요? by analogy with 'which exit' — but because Seoul exits are numbered, Koreans ask 몇 번 ('what number'), not 어느 ('which of an unspecified few'). Also never use 출구에서 나가요? — the direction particle is 로, not 에서.

word.en: Does this go to City Hall?
word.nuance: 직역하면 'This one — City Hall — does it go?' — a rapid boarding check fired at a bus driver or fellow passenger as you step on or approach. 이거 ('this one') points at the exact vehicle; the destination particle 에 is dropped in casual transit speech. Speech level: address the driver as 기사님 + 이거 시청 가요? (존댓말); between friends use 이거 시청 가? (반말). The near alternative expression is 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요?, which asks for general direction ('does it head toward City Hall?') rather than 'does it actually stop there' — use it when you only need to be in that area, not at the exact stop. Variant scale: 이거 시청 가요? → 이 버스 시청 가요? (specifying the vehicle) → 이거 시청 쪽으로 가요? (direction only). The English-speaker trap is over-formalizing: 이것은 시청에 갑니까? is grammatically correct but textbook-stiff and far too slow for a doorway. A crucial wrong form is 이거 시청 와요? — from the passenger's perspective the bus 가다 ('goes') there, not 오다 ('comes').

sentence.en: Driver, does this go to City Hall?

word.nuance: 직역하면 'At where do I change-and-ride?' — asked of station staff or a knowledgeable rider when your route requires a transfer. 갈아타다 is a compound verb formed from 갈다 ('replace/change') + 타다 ('ride'); it is far more natural than the clumsy paraphrase 버스를 바꿔서 타요. The transfer happens AT a station, so the location takes 에서 (contracted to 서 in 어디서): that 에서 is non-negotiable. Speech level is the ending: 갈아타요? (존댓말), 갈아타? (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 몇 호선으로 갈아타요?, which asks which LINE to switch to (note 으로, direction toward the line), versus 어디서 갈아타요? which asks the station — pick by what information you're missing. Variant scale: 어디서 갈아타요? → 어디서 갈아타야 돼요? (urgent) → 어디서 몇 호선으로 갈아타요? (asking both). The English-speaker pitfall is building 'transfer' from two English ideas: 버스를 바꿔서 타요 sounds like you're exchanging a physical ticket; the single idiomatic verb 갈아타다 is always the right choice.

options: May I ask you for directions?

word.nuance: 직역하면 'From here I get down' — 내리다 is the verb for alighting from any vehicle (bus, subway, taxi), and 여기서 (= 여기에서) marks the location of the alighting. The 에서 is non-negotiable: 내리다 takes the FROM/AT particle 에서, never the destination particle 에. Speech level shapes the nuance: 내릴게요 (using the 게 'I'll do it' ending) is the gentlest, warning fellow passengers to make room; 내려요 is a neutral polite statement; 내려 is casual (반말). The nearest alternative expression is 세워 주세요 ('please stop the vehicle'), which is directed at the driver — the dividing line is 내려요 announces YOUR own action while 세워 주세요 commands the driver's action; you often need both together. Variant scale: 내릴게요 (heads-up) → 내려요 (polite statement) → 내려 (반말) → 내려야 돼요 (urgent/forced). The English-speaker error is saying 여기서 나가요 for 'get out' — 나가다 is for exiting a building or room on foot; leaving a vehicle is always 내리다.

sentence.ko: A: 다음에서 내려요? / B: 아니요, 여기서 내려요. 지금이에요.

word.nuance: 직역하면 'The next station — where is it?' — asked of a fellow passenger when you've drifted or lost track of the stops. The crucial vocabulary: 역 means a train or subway station; on a bus the word is 정류장. Speech level is the ending: 어디예요? (존댓말, stranger or adult), 어디야? (반말, friend). The subject particle 이 is natural (다음 역이) but freely dropped in fast speech (다음 역 어디예요?). The nearest alternative expression is 다음이 무슨 역이에요?, which specifically asks for the station NAME (matches your map), whereas 어디예요? accepts either a name or a count ('two more stops') — the dividing line is precision of identity. Variant scale: 다음 역이 어디예요? → 다음이 무슨 역이에요? (name required) → 시청역 몇 정거장 남았어요? (count). English speakers sometimes ask 다음 역은 무엇입니까? — bookish and odd, because 무엇 fits objects, not places; use 어디 or 무슨 역 for station identity.

sentence.ko: 저기요, 다음 역이 어디예요? 제가 깜빡 졸았어요.
